title: Dock Edge Inc. (Jan 2019 TCC) Tax Court of Canada Case
subject: TCC appeal on whether a dock-hardware maker could prove technological uncertainty without expert or qualified technical testimony.
summary: Dock Edge + Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 11, is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision affecting Canadian corporations that claim SR&ED deductions and investment tax credits under the Income Tax Act. The Court dismissed DEI's appeal of $204,786 in denied expenditures because, without expert or qualified technical testimony, DEI could not establish what constituted routine engineering.
metaDescription: Explore the January 2019 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED ruling for Dock Edge Inc. and learn how it impacts Canadian R&D tax incentives.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Overview of the Dispute and Final Holding

On January 16, 2019, the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) issued its landmark Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) decision in Dock Edge + Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 11 (Docket: 2016-539(IT)G), presided over by Justice B. Russell. The Appellant, Dock Edge + Inc. (DEI), a privately held Canadian corporation headquartered in Ontario that manufactures and distributes marine and dockside hardware, appealed the reassessment by the Minister of National Revenue (the Minister) disallowing SR&ED tax incentives claimed for its 2011 taxation year ended August 31, 2011.

Following a General Procedure hearing in which the Appellant called two lay witnesses and the respondent Crown elected to call no witnesses at all, the Tax Court of Canada dismissed the appeal in its entirety, with costs awarded against the taxpayer. The ruling stands as a premier cautionary precedent in Canadian tax jurisprudence regarding the evidentiary burden required to establish the boundary between "routine engineering or standard procedures" and genuine "technological uncertainty" under the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) (the Act). Specifically, Justice Russell found a lack of evidence as to whether there were technical risks or uncertainties, essentially due to a lack of evidence as to what constituted routine engineering and standard procedures for the relevant technologies; while noting that experts are not necessarily required in SR&ED cases, he observed that they fill an evidentiary void where no persons having a relevant technical background who actively participated in the testing have testified, which was the case here.
The Taxpayer's SR&ED Claim and the Minister's Challenge

In its corporate tax filing for the fiscal period ended August 31, 2011, DEI claimed SR&ED expenditure deductions and associated Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) across five distinct commercial marine product and process development initiatives. The first initiative, Project One (Illuminating Dock Cleat Development), involved the design and physical integration of a solar-powered lighting assembly directly into a structural marine dock cleat. The second initiative, Project Two (Flush Mounted Dock Light Development), focused on the development of a low-profile, solar-powered lighting unit engineered to sit flush with the surface of a marine dock rather than protruding above the deck. The third initiative, Project Three (Boat Fender Valve Development), encompassed replacing the glued-in screw valve of DEI's air-leaking fenders with a basketball-style, self-sealing needle valve moulded directly into the material of DEI's rotational-moulded (roto-moulded) polyvinyl chloride (PVC) marine boat fenders. The fourth initiative, Project Four (Dock Bumper Corner Material Development), entailed investigating why certain moulded dock bumper corners were being returned looking as if they had been set on fire or damaged by ultraviolet (UV) radiation—a problem ultimately traced to the instability of the beige pigment when it reacted with sunlight and the UV inhibitors in the plastisol (liquid PVC moulding material), and resolved by adjusting the respective amounts of pigmentation, UV stabilizers and plastisol in the moulding compound for beige corners. Finally, Project Five (PVC/Plastisol Recycling Development) constituted a manufacturing process initiative aimed at recycling the cured scrap PVC ("regrind") generated during DEI's roto-moulding operations by using it, in combination with virgin PVC compound, in DEI's separate extrusion process (the eventual result being that this worked only for some bumpers not requiring particular hardness, and that only 10 percent of the roto-moulding waste could be used in the extrusion compound mixture).

body.text: Upon review by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the Minister reassessed DEI to deny the claimed SR&ED deductions and ITCs in full. The Minister's reassessment denied claimed qualified expenditures of $204,786 and ITCs of $71,675, and the issues before the Court were whether all or any of the five projects qualified as SR&ED and, if and to the extent so, whether three expenditure items specifically pleaded by the respondent were allowable—that is, whether the projects constituted eligible "experimental development" within the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the Act. The Crown maintained that DEI's activities did not satisfy the Northwest Hydraulic criteria, called no witnesses, and in argument on technological uncertainty relied on Joel Theatrical Rigging v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, and Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355, for the propositions that, without authoritative evidence of the techniques, procedures and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, the first criterion cannot be met, and that a failure on that criterion is dispositive.
Governing Canadian Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

In Canada, the federal R&D tax incentive regime is bifurcated into two primary statutory mechanisms within the Income Tax Act: subsection 37(1), which permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct qualifying current SR&ED expenditures in computing business income (or carry them forward indefinitely via an SR&ED expenditure pool), and section 127 (specifically subsections 127(5) and 127(9)), which grants Investment Tax Credits calculated as a percentage of qualified SR&ED expenditures that may be deducted from tax otherwise payable, with refunds of investment tax credits available to eligible taxpayers under section 127.1.

The substantive gateway to both provisions is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the Act. That provision defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". While paragraphs 248(1)(a) and (b) address basic and applied research, eligibility for commercial manufacturers such as DEI hinges on paragraph 248(1)(c)—experimental development—defined as "work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto". Once core experimental development is established, paragraph 248(1)(d) permits the inclusion of directly supporting work—specifically engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—provided such activities are "commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of" the core experimental work.

Because the statutory language of subsection 248(1) requires judicial interpretation to distinguish scientific investigation from commercial product development, Canadian courts uniformly apply the five-part legal test formulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), and subsequently affirmed as binding appellate law by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA). Under the Northwest Hydraulic doctrine, a taxpayer bears the legal burden of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that its claimed activities satisfy five sequential criteria. First, the taxpayer must establish whether there was a technical risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, the taxpayer must prove that the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the taxpayer must demonstrate that the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment. Fourth, the taxpayer must show that the process resulted in a technological advancement—meaning an advancement in general scientific or technological knowledge, rather than merely a new commercial product. Fifth, the taxpayer must verify that a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, the testing procedures, and the results was kept contemporaneously as the work progressed. In Dock Edge + Inc., Justice Russell systematically applied the Northwest Hydraulic framework to DEI's evidentiary record and concluded that the Appellant failed at the very first hurdle across all five projects and also failed the third (scientific method), fourth (technological advancement) and fifth (detailed records) criteria, while accepting on the second criterion that DEI's product development committee did develop theories or, loosely, hypotheses aimed at overcoming identified challenges.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

A rigorous legal and technical dissection of Justice Russell's Reasons for Judgment reveals six interconnected failures that doomed DEI's appeal. These failures illustrate how substantive technological deficiencies and procedural litigation missteps compound one another in General Procedure appeals before the Tax Court of Canada.
A. Failure to Establish the Baseline of "Routine Engineering or Standard Procedures"

The decisive legal failure in Dock Edge + Inc. centered on the first criterion of Northwest Hydraulic: proving the existence of a technological uncertainty. As formulated in Canadian jurisprudence and reflected in CRA administrative guidance, technological uncertainty exists only where whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, is not known or determinable on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience. Crucially, Northwest Hydraulic defines technological uncertainty by exclusion: a problem is only a technological uncertainty if it cannot be resolved by "routine engineering or standard procedures". If the resolution of a design flaw or manufacturing obstacle is doubtful solely because the taxpayer's specific personnel lack the requisite technical training or familiarity with existing engineering solutions, no true technological uncertainty exists in law.

Justice Russell articulated a profound evidentiary mandate that governs modern SR&ED litigation: to prove that a problem cannot be resolved by routine engineering or standard procedures, the taxpayer must first adduce credible evidence of what actually constitutes routine engineering and standard procedures in that specific technological domain. In dismissing DEI's appeal, Justice Russell stated directly that there was a "lack of evidence as to whether there were technical risks or uncertainties, essentially due to lack of evidence as to what constituted routine engineering and standard procedures for the relevant technologies".

Across Projects One and Two (the illuminating dock cleat and flush-mounted solar dock light), DEI's counsel argued that the projects involved the integration of standard technologies—for the cleat, the metallurgy of maintaining cleat strength and solar illumination technology—constituting a "system uncertainty" as described in 1726437 Ontario Inc. o/a Airmax Technologies v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 376, while the claimed uncertainty in Project Two concerned placing a solar light inside an aluminum structure in a marine environment subject to electrolysis and galvanic reactions. However, Justice Russell queried whether the cleat surmounted being a trivial combination of technologies—the light did its job and the cleat did its job, these being two separate jobs—and, for both projects, found that the Court lacked expert or equivalent evidence as to whether a meaningful, rather than trivial, integration of technologies was involved. Similarly, in Project Three (boat fender valve development, where needle-valve technology had long existed in basketballs) and Project Five (combining roto-moulding PVC regrind with virgin PVC in the extrusion process, which counsel briefly suggested also involved system uncertainty), there was no supporting evidence from any expert or participant with an adequate technical background; the Court also rejected counsel's submission that the "data" element of routine engineering means industry information and experience (such as Wally Szwez's 30 years in the marine and recreational industries), holding that "data" refers to measurements or observations and that relevant experience must be experience from which technical knowledge has been absorbed, not experience in an industry. Because no one competent to do so testified as to what were the routine engineering and standard procedures in the relevant technical fields (which Justice Russell identified as metallurgy and/or solar lighting), Justice Russell could not legally infer that DEI's difficulties were anything other than routine engineering adjustments.
B. Fatal Witness Selection and Evidentiary Deficits at Trial

The substantive failure to establish an engineering baseline was the direct consequence of DEI's litigation strategy and witness selection. At the hearing, DEI called only two witnesses: Michael Szwez (a lawyer by training and DEI director in charge of sales and marketing who managed the product development committee, a family member involved in DEI's operations, and son of company head Walter "Wally" Szwez) and George Prendergast (an employee of a DEI-related company with a long career in plastics production and sales, who described his role in four of the five projects as "oversight" at committee meetings, did not testify as an expert, and whose hours were not included in the claim).

This evidentiary posture suffered from three fatal flaws that crippled the Appellant's case. First, the testifying corporate witness lacked any technical credentials. As Justice Russell noted explicitly in the judgment, Michael Szwez possessed "no scientific or engineering" education, accreditation, or formal technical training. While a corporate executive can testify as a fact witness regarding business objectives, commercial timelines, and financial expenditures, a lay witness lacking scientific or engineering qualifications cannot credibly testify as to the limits of generally available scientific knowledge or the boundaries of routine engineering in polymer chemistry, rotational moulding thermodynamics, or optoelectronic packaging.

Second, DEI failed to call David Fleming, its former employee and subsequent consultant and the committee participant with the most relevant technical background. The evidentiary record revealed that Mr. Fleming, described in the SR&ED application as a "machinist, mechanic and industrial engineering technologist," was a regular attendee of DEI's product development committee meetings in 2011 and apparently had active participation in at least some of the five projects. Yet, inexplicably, DEI did not call Mr. Fleming as a witness at trial, nor did Appellant's counsel assert that Mr. Fleming was an engineer (although Michael Szwez said he thought he was). Apart from Michael Szwez, no member of the committee was called, nor any DEI employee or consultant with hands-on experience in or responsibility for DEI's production processes (including roto-moulding production manager Anthony Maccia, Sal Peruzza, who had 50 years of roto-moulding and extrusion experience, and the unnamed third party who developed the prototype dies), so that the Court heard little evidence as to specific testing methods and processes.

Third, there was a total absence of expert testimony. Neither party called an expert witness qualified under the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure). Although the Crown called no witnesses, the burden of proof remained on the Appellant, and Justice Russell observed that while experts are not necessarily necessary in SR&ED cases, they fill an evidentiary void where no persons having a relevant technical background and who actively participated in the testing have testified, which was the case here. As Justice Russell emphasized regarding Project Two, "Again we lacked expert or equivalent evidence" as to whether the project involved an integration of technologies at all and, if so, of a meaningful rather than trivial nature.
C. Conflation of Commercial Management Frameworks ("PDCA") with the Scientific Method

Under the second and third criteria of Northwest Hydraulic, a taxpayer must formulate specific scientific or technological hypotheses aimed at resolving the identified uncertainty and test those hypotheses through a systematic investigation governed by the "total discipline of the scientific method". This requires procedures according with established and objective principles of scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses.

At trial, Michael Szwez testified that DEI conducted its development projects using the "PDCA" approach, which he defined for the Court as "Plan, Develop, Conclude/Correct, Act" (a modified variant of the classic Deming quality control cycle: Plan-Do-Check-Act). DEI attempted to equate this commercial product management cycle with the systematic investigation required by subsection 248(1) of the Act. Justice Russell accepted that the committee approached project development in an organized and logical way using the corporate PDCA approach (which Michael Szwez described in cross-examination as a quality management system that a company would have in place), but held that this was not enough to equate with the discipline of the scientific method. Adhering to a structured business or quality-assurance routine—such as planning a product feature, developing a physical prototype, observing whether it functions in a commercial setting, and correcting defects—does not constitute the scientific method. As highlighted in Northwest Hydraulic and reiterated in the jurisprudence surrounding Dock Edge + Inc., what distinguishes routine activity from SR&ED "is not solely the adherence to systematic routines, but the adoption of the entire scientific method... with a view to removing a technological uncertainty through the formulation and testing of innovative and untested hypotheses". Although the Court accepted that the committee developed theories or, loosely, hypotheses, no records were kept detailing committee discussions (whiteboard notes were soon erased), no records of hypotheses and tests were produced, testing relied heavily on trials at the family cottage in Georgian Bay and on customer feedback from some 3,000 prototype-style cleats sold through DEI's network (Michael Szwez conceded these were not always controlled tests), and the Court heard little about DEI's procedures; Justice Russell noted that had detailed minutes and records of hypotheses and tests been kept, this criterion could likely have been established.
D. Outsourcing of Core Formulation and Unstructured Trial-and-Error with Suppliers

Third-party involvement in DEI's materials work arose in Project Three (boat fender valve development) and Project Four (dock bumper corner material development), although, as explained below, Justice Russell made no finding that these arrangements were themselves disqualifying. In Project Four, DEI investigated why beige dock bumper corners were being returned looking burnt or UV-damaged; field testing disproved its initial dock-stain hypothesis, other testing ruled out the moulding process, and the committee concluded it was a pigment issue. The evidence established that DEI moulds, but does not make, the pigment, which is purchased for DEI to apply, and the matter was referred to a third-party laboratory that found the beige pigment unstable not during moulding but when it reacted with sunlight and the UV inhibitors in the plastisol. It was in Project Three (the fender valve), not Project Four, that DEI's materials supplier made up plastisol compositions of differing hardness, which DEI's group, including production manager Anthony Maccia and Sal Peruzza, tested through the moulding process until an acceptable composition and process were found.

Justice Russell, however, made no finding that these supplier or laboratory arrangements created a legal vulnerability under subsections 37(1) or 248(1) of the Act; his reasons do not address third-party performance of SR&ED at all. On the record, the Project Four hypotheses (dock stain, moulding process, pigment) were developed by DEI's own committee, and because DEI's material compound supplier had never heard of the problem, it was left to DEI to pursue it, which DEI resolved by adjusting the respective amounts of pigmentation, UV stabilizers and plastisol. The decision contains no findings on whether DEI knew or directed its supplier's formulations; what it records is that the only documentation for Project Four was three pages of handwritten notes, attributed to Mr. Fleming, appearing to reference steps taken between March and August 2011, and Mr. Fleming did not testify. In Project Three, the acceptable material composition and moulding process were reached through testing of composition variations and substantial customer field testing, yet neither Mr. Maccia nor Mr. Peruzza was called to give evidence. The Court's concern was therefore evidentiary rather than contractual: the persons with hands-on involvement in the materials work did not testify and no detailed records were kept; documenting third-party work under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) (SR&ED carried on on behalf of the taxpayer), with full disclosure of parameters and protocols, is prudent practice but was not an issue decided in this appeal.
E. Absence of Technological Advancement vs. Incremental Commercial Product Creation

Under the fourth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic, the work must seek and achieve a "technological advancement". In Dock Edge + Inc., DEI's counsel submitted that DEI had achieved technological advancements because the knowledge it acquired was not generally accessible to a competent professional in the field, although no evidence was led supporting that proposition; the record also showed that the illuminating dock cleat was ultimately included in DEI's commercial offerings. DEI's counsel asked what DEI had learned in the projects, but did not ask whether, and if so what, general knowledge new to the pertinent scientific community had been developed; Justice Russell found no informed testimony indicating that DEI had advanced general understanding, as distinguished from its own specific knowledge.

Justice Russell clarified the strict legal boundary between a new commercial product and a technological advancement, holding that "a technological advancement is achieved actually when general knowledge has been advanced through application of the scientific method". While commending DEI on its innovative approach and success in developing new or improved commercial products, Justice Russell adopted the reasoning in Zeuter Development Corp. v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, that novelty or innovation in a product is not sufficient to illustrate technological advancement; what matters is whether those features arose through the process of SR&ED. Thus, even if a product is new to the taxpayer's catalog or, as DEI understood of its illuminated cleat, without any known comparable product, it does not represent a technological advancement unless the process advances general understanding in the field, as distinguished from the taxpayer's own specific knowledge.
F. Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation

Finally, under the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic, DEI failed to maintain detailed, contemporaneous documentation recording hypotheses, experimental methodologies, quantitative test data, and analytical conclusions as the work progressed during the 2011 fiscal year. The evidence was that no records were kept detailing discussions at the product development committee meetings held in 2011 (which Mr. Fleming attended), that whiteboard notes were soon erased, and that the Court heard "little evidence as to specific testing methods and/or processes"; only a few photographs of prototypes and three pages of handwritten notes for one project were entered in evidence, leading Justice Russell to answer this criterion with a definite no.

Furthermore, oral testimony from a director without scientific or engineering training, supported by Mr. Prendergast (whose role was described as oversight at committee meetings and whose fact evidence was not appreciably different), could not cure the absence of primary, dated records; Justice Russell distinguished ACSIS EHR (Electronic Health Record) Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 263, where significant contemporaneous records were combined with ample oral testimony from the trained technicians who carried out the work. As Justice Russell's ruling confirms, while detailed records are not an absolute legal requirement, their presence is indicative of the scientific methodology, and, as stated in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA) and adopted in Zeuter, documentary evidence is the only reliable method of demonstrating that research was undertaken in a systematic fashion.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the Northwest Hydraulic doctrine against Dock Edge + Inc.'s specific failures and the evidentiary standard of proof enforced by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Dock Edge + Inc. (2019 TCC 11)
The Court's Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Mandate

cells: 1. Existence of Technological Risk or Uncertainty (Distinction from Routine Engineering)
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 1; C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (FCA)

Failed across all 5 projects (illuminating cleat, flush light, fender valve, bumper corner pigment, PVC regrind) to prove what constituted "routine engineering or standard procedures" in the relevant technical fields (identified by the Court as metallurgy and/or solar lighting). Relied on a lay witness (M. Szwez) with no scientific or engineering training, failed to call internal engineering technologist D. Fleming, and called no expert witnesses.

Objective Baseline Proof: The taxpayer must establish, via qualified technical fact witnesses or independent expert testimony, the objective state of generally available scientific/engineering knowledge and standard industry procedures. Only by proving where routine engineering ends can the Court find that an obstacle constituted a true technological uncertainty.
2. Formulation of Scientific or Technological Hypotheses
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 2

Michael Szwez tended to refer to project goals or targets as "hypotheses" and to obstacles ("challenges") as technological uncertainties; nonetheless, the Court accepted that the committee did develop theories or, loosely, hypotheses aimed at overcoming identified challenges, and did not decide the appeal on this criterion. In Project 4, the hypotheses (dock stain, moulding process, pigment) were DEI's own, with a third-party laboratory engaged for pigment testing; supplier-made plastisol compositions featured in Project 3, not in the pigment project.

Causal & Testable Proposition: The taxpayer must prove that it (or a contracted performer acting under its technical direction) formulated explicit, testable causal propositions prior to experimentation that link specific independent technological variables to dependent physical or chemical outcomes aimed at eliminating the uncertainty.
3. Accordance with the Scientific Method (Systematic Investigation)
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 3

Relied on a commercial management / quality control framework termed "PDCA" (Plan, Develop, Conclude/Correct, Act) described by M. Szwez. Relied heavily on informal testing at the family cottage in Georgian Bay and on customer field feedback (including some 3,000 prototype-style cleats sold, with about 150 customers reporting problems), which Michael Szwez conceded were not always controlled tests; kept no records of committee discussions, hypotheses or tests, and the Court heard little about the procedures used.

Total Discipline of the Scientific Method: Adherence to business or manufacturing routines (like PDCA) is legally insufficient. The taxpayer must prove procedures according with established and objective principles of scientific method—trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses; Justice Russell noted that detailed minutes and records of hypotheses and tests could likely have established this criterion.
4. Achievement of Technological Advancement
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 4

Argued that DEI achieved technological advancements because the knowledge it acquired was not generally accessible to a competent professional in the field, but adduced no evidence supporting that proposition. Counsel's questions addressed what DEI itself had learned, not whether general knowledge new to the pertinent scientific community had been developed.

Advancement of General Knowledge: Justice Russell held that a technological advancement is achieved only when general knowledge in a field of science or technology has been advanced through the application of the scientific method. Citing Zeuter, novelty or innovation in a product is not sufficient; what matters is whether the features arose through the process of SR&ED.
5. Contemporaneous Documentation
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1); Zeuter; RIS-Christie (FCA); ACSIS (distinguished); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 5

Kept no records detailing 2011 committee discussions (whiteboard notes were erased); only a few photographs of prototypes and three pages of handwritten notes for one project (Project 4) were entered in evidence. Relied on oral testimony from a non-technical director and from G. Prendergast (oversight role at committee meetings; not an expert), without testimony from the technical personnel who carried out the work.

Dated, Specific Empirical Records: Although detailed records are not strictly a legal requirement and oral testimony can suffice when given by trained participants and supported by significant contemporaneous records (ACSIS), the prudent taxpayer should maintain contemporaneous, dated documentation generated as the work progressed—specifically recording the baseline literature/engineering review, each hypothesis, experimental parameters, quantitative test results, and analytical conclusions.
6. Commensurate Supporting Work & Third-Party Boundaries
Income Tax Act, s. 37(1), s. 248(1)(d)

Not reached: because the projects were not shown to be SR&ED, the Court did not rule on the three expenditure items specifically pleaded by the respondent; Mr. Prendergast's hours were not included in the claim, and no finding was made on the supplier (Project 3) or third-party laboratory (Project 4) involvement.

Strict Nexus to Eligible Core Work: Supporting activities (design, moulding trials, testing) under para. 248(1)(d) are eligible only if they are commensurate with the needs and directly in support of eligible experimental development under para. 248(1)(c). Paragraph 248(1)(f) separately excludes quality control or routine testing; the Court expressly did not consider the commercial-production exclusion because the respondent had not pleaded it, and made no ruling on vendor sample testing.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the legal holdings of Dock Edge + Inc. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 11) into actionable tax and engineering governance, the following two applied industry case studies model projects that face the exact legal and evidentiary pitfalls identified by Justice Russell. Each case study provides a comprehensive, step-by-step remedial restructuring blueprint designed to withstand CRA technical review and Tax Court of Canada scrutiny.
Case Study 1: Polymer Recycling & Custom Plastisol Compounding in Rotational Moulding
Scenario & Vulnerability Profile (Mirroring Projects 3, 4, and 5 of Dock Edge + Inc.)

Laurentian Marine Polymers Inc. ("Laurentian"), an Ontario-based Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC), manufactures heavy-duty rotational-moulded marine fenders and dock corner bumpers. In its current fiscal year, Laurentian initiates a project to incorporate 35% post-industrial cross-linked and plasticized PVC scrap ("regrind") from rejected boat fenders back into virgin liquid plastisol to roto-mould high-impact dock bumper corners and integrated inflation valves.

At the outset of the engagement, Laurentian exhibits vulnerabilities analogous to the evidentiary weaknesses that proved fatal in Dock Edge + Inc. First, Laurentian does not compound its own plastisol; it informally asks its chemical resin supplier (ChemCorp) to send over tweaked liquid plastisol batches while Laurentian runs shop-floor moulding trials to see if the parts crack. Second, Laurentian's plant manager (who holds a business diploma rather than an engineering degree) tracks progress using an internal "PDCA" quality board (Plan, Develop, Conclude, Act). Third, no baseline study exists showing why blending 35% cured PVC regrind into liquid plastisol cannot be achieved through standard polymer processing procedures.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance & Establishing the "Routine Engineering" Baseline

To overcome Justice Russell's threshold objection—that the Court cannot find technological uncertainty without evidence of what constitutes routine engineering and standard procedures—Laurentian must formalize technical leadership and document the state of the art before commencing shop-floor trials. Laurentian must immediately appoint an internal Professional Engineer (P.Eng. in Chemical or Polymer Engineering) or a qualified senior Polymer Technologist as the Principal Investigator (PI). Governance protocols must mandate that this individual leads all technical committee meetings, authors the experimental protocols, and remains available to testify at both CRA Science Reviews and any subsequent Tax Court hearing, thereby avoiding the evidentiary gap created by the failure to call industrial engineering technologist David Fleming in Dock Edge + Inc.

Prior to formulating any hypotheses, the PI must compile and archive a formal, dated "Baseline State-of-Technology Dossier." This technical memorandum must cite polymer engineering textbooks, peer-reviewed literature, ASTM standards, and vendor technical data sheets demonstrating why standard rotational moulding procedures fail at a 35% regrind loading. Specifically, the dossier will establish that in standard polymer engineering, previously fused PVC regrind possesses a degraded thermal stability profile and lacks free liquid plasticizer solvation sites; consequently, standard mechanical mixing above a 10% to 12% weight fraction induces phase separation, sharp plastisol viscosity spikes (η > 8,000 cP), and interfacial void formation during biaxial rotation. Furthermore, the dossier must prove through initial benchmark calculations that routine processing adjustments—such as increasing oven residence time, altering biaxial rotation ratios from 4:1 to 2:1, or adding conventional dioctyl terephthalate (DOTP) plasticizer—fail to achieve homogeneous fusion at a 35% regrind loading without triggering thermal dehydrochlorination (burning) of the virgin matrix. This archived dossier provides the exact objective evidence missing in Dock Edge + Inc., proving to the CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and the Tax Court where "routine engineering" ends and genuine "technological uncertainty" begins.
Step 2: Rewriting Supplier Contract Terms & IP/Technical Control

In Dock Edge + Inc., DEI's supplier made up the Project 3 plastisol compositions and a third-party laboratory performed the Project 4 pigment testing; although Justice Russell made no finding that these arrangements were disqualifying, the people with hands-on involvement did not testify and the Court heard little evidence of specific testing methods. Laurentian must restructure its legal and technical relationship with ChemCorp to ensure that the formulation of scientific hypotheses and control over chemical variables reside legally with Laurentian.

Where ChemCorp acts strictly as a custom blender, Laurentian must execute a Master Toll-Compounding and Technical Disclosure Agreement. Under this contract, Laurentian's PI retains total scientific control over the independent chemical variables, instructing ChemCorp in writing to compound exact quantitative chemical formulations specified by Laurentian (detailing exact weight percentages of emulsion-grade PVC resin, specific molecular weight polymeric plasticizers, epoxidized soybean oil co-stabilizers, and cryogenic regrind particle distributions). The contract must legally obligate ChemCorp to disclose full Certificates of Analysis (CoA) and exact chemical batch records for every experimental run, closing the kind of evidentiary gap on material composition and testing methods that left Justice Russell with little evidence as to specific testing methods.

Conversely, if ChemCorp's polymer chemists actively assist in formulating the chemical hypotheses, Laurentian must execute a formal Canadian SR&ED Subcontract Agreement with ChemCorp (assuming ChemCorp is a taxable Canadian supplier performing the work within Canada). This agreement must explicitly state that ChemCorp is performing experimental polymer compounding on behalf of Laurentian within the meaning of subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) of the Income Tax Act. It must vest 100% of the resulting intellectual property, chemical formulation data, and experimental test logs in Laurentian, require ChemCorp to issue itemized invoices separating eligible experimental compounding labour and materials from commercial production batches, and obligate ChemCorp's lead chemist to participate in CRA technical interviews and provide witness testimony in the Tax Court of Canada if required.
Step 3: Transforming "PDCA" into a Structured Process of Scientific Experimentation

Laurentian must abolish the "Plan, Develop, Conclude, Act" management terminology for R&D projects and replace it with a rigorous Design of Experiments (DoE) protocol governed by the total discipline of the scientific method. Every experimental cycle must begin with a documented, falsifiable causal hypothesis authored by the PI prior to compounding. For example, Hypothesis H-01 must state that cryogenically pulverizing cured PVC regrind to a narrow particle size distribution (D<sub>90</sub> < 150 μm) and pre-treating the regrind surface with a 2.5 wt% aminosilane coupling agent prior to dispersion in a low-molecular-weight benzoate plasticizer will create covalent interfacial bridging across the virgin-regrind boundary, maintaining plastisol Brookfield viscosity below 4,500 cP at 23°C and achieving a tensile elongation at break exceeding 220% in the moulded bumper corner.

Instead of moulding parts to see if they "look acceptable" on the shop floor, Laurentian must execute controlled DoE matrices where independent variables are systematically isolated and tested against quantitative dependent metrics.

cells: Series 1A–1D (Baseline Verification)
Untreated mechanical regrind (D<sub>90</sub> = 850 μm) at 15%, 25%, 35% wt; standard DOTP plasticizer; PIAT 205°C.
Brookfield RV viscosity (cP); ASTM D412 tensile strength (MPa); cross-sectional optical microscopy void count.
Hypothesis Falsified: Above 15% wt, viscosity exceeded 9,200 cP and incomplete sinter fusion caused 18% porosity, confirming standard procedures fail.
Series 2A–2F (Particle Size & Solvation)
Cryogenic regrind (D<sub>90</sub> = 140 μm) at 35% wt; fast-fusing dibenzoate co-plasticizer blend (10–30 phr); PIAT 212°C.
Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) storage modulus; Brookfield viscosity aging over 48 hours; Shore A hardness.
Partial Validation: Viscosity stabilized at 4,100 cP, but interfacial delamination occurred under impact due to poor surface wetting of cross-linked particles.
Series 3A–3H (Interfacial Coupling)
Cryogenic regrind (D<sub>90</sub> = 140 μm) at 35% wt; 1.0% to 3.5% wt aminosilane surface functionalization; wireless telemetry oven profiling.
ASTM D412 elongation at break (%); scanning electron microscopy (SEM) fracture surface analysis; valve burst pressure (kPa).
Hypothesis Confirmed: At 2.5% wt silane coupling and 218°C peak internal air temperature, covalent bridging eliminated boundary voids, advancing polymer recycling knowledge.

body.text: Step 4: Contemporaneous Documentation Architecture

To satisfy Criterion 5 of Northwest Hydraulic and avoid Justice Russell's critique regarding uncorroborated 2011 committee meetings, Laurentian must implement a mandatory digital Electronic Laboratory Notebook (ELN) and structured R&D repository. Unlike DEI's undocumented committee meetings, every technical review meeting at Laurentian must generate a timestamped record signed by the PI, explicitly logging why the previous test run failed to validate the hypothesis, what chemical or thermodynamic anomaly occurred, and how the hypothesis is being modified for the next iteration. Simultaneously, Laurentian must implement contemporaneously approved financial timesheets and batch cards that segregate eligible paragraph 248(1)(c) and (d) experimental moulding runs (such as 4.5 hours running DoE Series 3B with wireless telemetry sensors) from routine commercial production or routine mould maintenance.
Case Study 2: Mechatronic & Optoelectronic Integration in Harsh Marine Hardware
Scenario & Vulnerability Profile (Mirroring Projects 1 and 2 of Dock Edge + Inc.)

Pacific Mooring Systems Ltd. ("Pacific"), a Canadian marine hardware manufacturer based in British Columbia, initiates a project to develop an autonomous, structural solar-illuminated mooring cleat and a flush-mounted dock deck beacon capable of withstanding 35,000 N of dynamic hawser mooring shear load while maintaining IP68 hermetically sealed optoelectronic performance under continuous saltwater immersion and freeze-thaw thermal cycling (−30°C to +55°C).

Without remedial intervention, Pacific's project mirrors Projects 1 and 2 of Dock Edge + Inc. Pacific's industrial designers assemble off-the-shelf solar cells, lithium-iron-phosphate (LiFePO4) batteries, and LEDs into CAD-designed aluminum and polycarbonate housings. When water leaks into the flush housing or the cleat cracks under load, the team iteratively changes gasket thicknesses or wall dimensions by trial and error ("PDCA"). Furthermore, Pacific intends to claim the entire commercial product development lifecycle as SR&ED, operating under the misconception that because an illuminated structural cleat is a novel commercial product, the design work automatically qualifies as a technological advancement.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance & Isolating Core SR&ED from Industrial Design

In Dock Edge + Inc., DEI adduced no expert or equivalent evidence distinguishing what may have been a trivial combination of technologies (fitting a solar light into a cleat or flush dock mount) from genuine technological uncertainty. Pacific must establish a strict "Technical Eligibility Firewall" at project inception. Pacific's engineering governance charter must explicitly classify standard CAD mechanical layout, commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) solar panel selection, basic PCB routing, cosmetic industrial design, and standard waterproofing via conventional elastomeric O-rings as non-eligible routine engineering. Excluding these routine product development activities upfront establishes analytical credibility with the CRA and prevents the contamination of the core claim.

Next, Pacific's lead Mechanical and Materials Engineer (P.Eng.) must author a dated "Baseline Engineering Conflict Analysis" demonstrating a fundamental physical antagonism (systemic trade-off) that cannot be resolved via standard engineering handbooks or conventional finite element analysis (FEA) libraries. Specifically, the analysis will document that structural mooring cleats require high-modulus metallic alloys (such as 316L stainless steel or anodized 6061-T6 aluminum) to resist 35 kN dynamic shock loads, whereas the flush optical window over the photovoltaic cell requires an optically transparent polymer (> 88% light transmittance across 400–1100 nm). However, the severe coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) mismatch between the metallic structural body (α ≈ 23 × 10<sup>−6</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>) and optically transparent polymers (α ≈ 65–70 × 10<sup>−6</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>), combined with elastic micro-strain deformation (> 0.4% strain) of the cleat horn under dynamic hawser tension, causes immediate interfacial delamination of standard marine structural adhesives and catastrophic failure of conventional compression seals during −30°C freeze-thaw cycles. Consequently, rather than claiming "the development of an illuminating dock cleat" (which Justice Russell queried as possibly a trivial combination of technologies—the light doing its job and the cleat doing its own—in the absence of expert or equivalent evidence), Pacific defines its SR&ED project strictly as an experimental investigation of stress-decoupled, CTE-compensated metal-to-optical-polymer hermetic bonding architectures under coupled cyclic structural strain and cryogenic thermal shock.
Step 2: Implementing a Rigorous Scientific Experimentation & Hypothesis Tracking Protocol

To satisfy Criteria 2, 3, and 4 of Northwest Hydraulic and prove that general technological knowledge is being advanced through the scientific method, Pacific's engineers must formulate mathematical and materials science hypotheses prior to physical fabrication. For instance, Hypothesis H-02 states that introducing a laser-microtextured gradient transition zone on the 6061-T6 aluminum cleat recess coupled with a dual-modulus interpenetrating polymer network (IPN) urethane-silicone adhesive layer of 1.2 mm thickness will dissipate shear strain energy during 35 kN load spikes without exceeding the cohesive peel threshold of the polycarbonate optical lens across −30°C to +55°C thermal cycling.

Instead of placing prototypes on a dock and waiting to observe water ingress (unstructured trial-and-error), Pacific must construct an instrumented laboratory test protocol recording quantitative time-series data. Each experimental iteration must capture biaxial strain gauge telemetry measuring micro-strain (με) at the metal-polymer interface under simulated hydraulic actuator hawser loading, helium mass spectrometry hermeticity leak rates (< 1 × 10−7 mbar·L/s) before and after 100 thermal shock cycles in an environmental chamber, and spectroradiometric measurements of optical attenuation through the stressed polymer window. Even when an experimental iteration fails—for instance, if cohesive fracture occurs at −22°C due to glass-transition embrittlement of the urethane phase—the empirical characterization of why that failure occurred advances Pacific's technological knowledge base regarding multi-material marine interfaces, satisfying Justice Russell's requirement that "general knowledge has been advanced through application of the scientific method".
Step 3: Contractual & Evidentiary Readiness for CRA Review and Tax Court Litigation

To insulate the claim against the evidentiary collapse witnessed in Dock Edge + Inc., Pacific must structure its external testing contracts and internal litigation files with precision. Where Pacific utilizes a third-party Canadian university laboratory or environmental testing facility to perform cyclic tensile loading or thermal shock chamber testing, the written contract must specify that the testing constitutes commensurate supporting work (data collection and testing) under paragraph 248(1)(d) directed exclusively by Pacific's P.Eng., with raw sensor data files (CSV and TDMS logs), equipment calibration certificates, and failure micrographs delivered directly into Pacific's contemporaneous archive.

Finally, Pacific must maintain a "Litigation-Ready Technical File" for each taxation year. This archive must contain the curriculum vitae and professional engineering credentials of every internal technical lead, signed contemporaneous experiment logs, and a preserved physical repository of failed and succeeded experimental test coupons tagged by test run number. Should a dispute proceed to the Tax Court of Canada under the General Procedure, Pacific will present its internal P.Eng. as a primary technical fact witness alongside an independent, Rule-compliant Expert Witness (such as an academic specialist in marine materials engineering) to establish the objective baseline of routine engineering—directly neutralizing the Crown's litigation strategy in Dock Edge + Inc.
5. Strategic Synthesis for Canadian SR&ED Practitioners

The Tax Court of Canada's ruling in Dock Edge + Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 11, reinforces a vital doctrinal reality of Canadian tax law: the SR&ED tax incentive program under sections 37, 127, and 248(1) of the Income Tax Act is not a subsidy for commercial innovation, industrial design, or manufacturing modernization. It is a rigorously policed statutory incentive reserved exclusively for taxpayers who encounter genuine scientific or technological limits and systematically advance general technological knowledge through the discipline of the scientific method.

As Justice Russell's decision demonstrates, the battlefield in Canadian SR&ED disputes has shifted decisively toward threshold baseline proof. A taxpayer that enters a CRA review or a Tax Court of Canada courtroom armed only with lay business testimony, commercial quality-control acronyms ("PDCA"), unrecorded committee meetings and erased whiteboards, and no testimony from the technical personnel who actually performed the work will inevitably fail to discharge its burden of proof. Conversely, by establishing an objective, documented baseline of standard engineering practice prior to experimentation, retaining contractual and scientific control over third-party material formulations, enforcing quantitative hypothesis testing, and preserving qualified technical witnesses, Canadian enterprises can robustly defend their SR&ED claims at every administrative and judicial level.

outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; without expert evidence the taxpayer could not show what went beyond routine engineering.
